textShort: Step outside and watch the sunrise or sunset.
textLong: Acts can be for you, too. Step outside (or to a window) and actually watch the sky change as the sun comes up or goes down. Put your phone away for a few minutes and just take it in. If you want, snap a quick photo of the sky as your act memory.

textShort: Send a friend a funny meme or video to make them laugh.
textLong: Find something that genuinely made you laugh—a meme, a clip, or a silly photo—and send it to a friend just to brighten their day. No agenda, no reply needed; just a little joy passed along.

textShort: Take a 10-minute walk and notice three things you've never seen before.
textLong: Head out for a short walk—around the block, campus, or a nearby path—and slow down enough to spot three things you have never noticed: a funny sign, a cool plant, a hidden detail on a building. It is a tiny adventure that resets your head. Snap a photo of one of your finds as your act memory.

textShort: Water a plant—or talk to it!
textLong: Give a plant a little love today: water it, move it toward the light, dust off its leaves, or just say hi. Caring for something living is a small, grounding act of kindness toward the world around you. Snap a photo of your plant as your act memory if you like.

textShort: Write down three things that went well today.
textLong: Before the day ends, jot down three things that went well—big or tiny. A good meal, a laugh, finishing a task, a kind word. Noticing the good on purpose makes more of it stand out tomorrow.

textShort: Spend 15 minutes on a hobby you keep "not having time" for.
textLong: Pick that hobby you always say you will get back to—drawing, an instrument, a game, writing, building something—and give it 15 honest minutes today. No pressure to be productive or good; just enjoy it. Snap a photo of what you made or did as your act memory.

textShort: Plan and cook a brand-new recipe.
textLong: Pick a recipe you have never made, grab what you need, and cook it this week. It does not have to turn out perfectly—the fun is in trying something new in the kitchen. Take a photo of your finished dish as your act memory.

textShort: Have a screen-free evening—board game, puzzle, or a book.
textLong: Pick one evening this week to put the screens away. Play a board game, do a puzzle, read, or just talk. Notice how different a night feels without scrolling. Snap a photo of how you spent it as your act memory.

textShort: Host or join a game night with friends.
textLong: Round up a few friends for a game night—board games, cards, video games, or trivia. Keep it easy and fun; the point is time together and a lot of laughing. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Make something and give it away.
textLong: Create something with your hands this month—art, baked goods, a craft, a playlist, anything—and give it away to someone with no strings attached. Making and giving is twice the joy. Take a photo of what you made as your act memory.

textShort: Do today's Wordle or Connections with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Ask a friend if they want to solve today’s NYT Wordle or Connections on one phone (in person or on a call). Work through it together—no spoilers for people not playing. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Play one round of GeoGuessr together—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Open GeoGuessr (or a similar map quiz) and pass one phone back and forth with a friend for five minutes. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Rock–paper–scissors best-of-three with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Challenge a friend to a quick best-of-three rock–paper–scissors. Keep it light and silly. Winner gets nothing except bragging rights; loser owes a genuine compliment. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Play two truths and a lie with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: With a friend, each share two true facts and one lie; the other guesses the lie. Swap roles once. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Play 20 questions about a friend's hobby—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Ask a friend to pick a hobby or interest you do not know much about. You get up to 20 yes-or-no questions to guess it. When you figure it out (or run out of questions), let them tell you one fun fact about it. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Pass a phone around and build a one-sentence story—and take a picture together after!
textLong: With three or more friends at lunch or hanging out, open Notes and add one sentence each, passing the phone around until the story feels complete (at least four sentences). When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Order the barista's favorite drink—and take a picture together after!
textLong: At a café, ask the barista what they would order for themselves today (or their off-menu favorite). Order it if you can, thank them by name if they shared it, and tip if possible. When you are done, take a picture together afterward—your drinks on the counter or with the barista only if they are happy to be in it—and save it as your act memory.

textShort: Pantry cook-off with someone you live with—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Pick five ingredients you both already have at home. Set a 20-minute timer and each make a small plate for the other. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Snack trade at lunch with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: At lunch, trade one snack item with a friend (sealed or clearly yours). Chat while you eat. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Blind tea or coffee taste-test for two—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Make three small cups of tea or coffee at home for a friend (or someone you live with). Blindfold or look away while tasting; rank them together. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Play UNO with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Bring a deck of UNO or a simple card game and invite a friend to one quick round at lunch or while hanging out. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Compliment the person on your left in a friend group—and take a picture together after!
textLong: With at least three friends, go around once: everyone gives one specific, kind compliment to the person on their left (no body shaming, no backhanded jokes). When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Teach each other a 30-second dance move—and take a picture together after!
textLong: With a friend, each teach the other one short dance move (from a video, sport warmup, or silly freestyle). Practice until you can do both in a row. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Mini scavenger hunt with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Agree on a 10-minute list (e.g. something blue, something funny, something older than you, something that feels like kindness). Hunt together in a mall, campus, or neighborhood. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Voice-note-only day with friends—and take a picture together after!
textLong: With two or three close friends, pick one day where your group chat is voice memos only—no text. Check in, joke, encourage. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Host a local multiplayer game night—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Invite a friend over (or use a shared screen) for one session of Mario Kart, Jackbox, or any same-room multiplayer game. If a guest wins, they pick the next round. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Teach a relative one phone trick they wanted—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Ask a parent, grandparent, or older relative what one phone thing confuses them—shared albums, Wordle, focus mode, photos backup. Walk them through it until they do one step solo. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Interview a grandparent or elder relative—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Ask five questions: childhood memory, proudest moment, best advice, funniest family story, and what kindness means to them. Listen without interrupting. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Family show-and-tell night—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Get everyone at home to bring one object with a 60-second story. No interrupting during stories. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Play chess or checkers with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: Bring a board or use a table at home, school, or the park. Play a quick game with a friend—set a 15-minute cap if you are short on time. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Give a friend a compliment and ask about their week—and take a picture together after!
textLong: With a friend, offer one genuine compliment, then ask: “What was the best part of your week?” Listen for at least a minute without looking at your phone. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Swap “song of the day” with a friend—and take a picture together after!
textLong: With a friend, in person or on a call, each play 30 seconds of a song that matches your mood today. Explain why you picked it. When you are done, take a picture together afterward and save it as your act memory (faces only with everyone's permission).

textShort: Thank one of your closest friends over text!
textLong: Take a moment to reflect on one of your closest friends—the person who has been there for you through thick and thin. Now, send them a thoughtful text message expressing your gratitude. Let them know how much their friendship means to you, recall a specific memory or moment you appreciated, and tell them the impact they have had on your life. A simple, heartfelt message can brighten their day and strengthen your bond. Optional: save a screenshot or photo that reminds you of them as your act memory.

textShort: Text a family member you have not talked to lately.
textLong: Think of a parent, grandparent, aunt, uncle, or cousin you have been meaning to reach out to. Send a short, warm message—ask how they are, share something small from your day, or thank them for something they did for you. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Say thank you to someone who helped you today.
textLong: Notice someone who made your day easier—a teacher, cashier, bus driver, coworker, or friend. Look them in the eye (or write it clearly) and thank them for something specific they did.

textShort: Share something you are grateful for with a friend.
textLong: Gratitude grows when it is shared. Tell a friend one thing you are thankful for today—it can be about them, your health, a meal, or a small moment that went well. Invite them to share one back if they want.

textShort: Offer your seat or give up your spot for someone.
textLong: On transit, in a waiting room, or at an event, offer your seat or step aside so someone who needs it more can be comfortable—an older adult, someone with heavy bags, or a parent with young kids.

textShort: Water a plant or care for something living at home.
textLong: Take a minute to water a houseplant, refill a pet’s water bowl with extra care, or tidy a small garden patch. Caring for living things is a quiet act of responsibility and kindness.

textShort: Leave a positive review or comment for a small business.
textLong: Think of a local café, shop, or service you genuinely like. Leave a short, honest review online or send them a kind message. Small businesses often remember encouragement for years. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Do a chore without being asked.
textLong: Notice something that needs doing at home—dishes, trash, tidying a shared space, or folding laundry—and do it before someone has to remind you. A small surprise can ease stress for everyone you live with.

textShort: Ask someone how their day really went—and listen.
textLong: Pick one person and ask, “How was your day?” Give them space to answer without rushing to fix or compare. Listening well is one of the kindest gifts you can give.

textShort: Share a snack or treat with someone nearby.
textLong: If you have something extra—a piece of fruit, a cookie, or part of your lunch—offer to share with a sibling, roommate, classmate, or coworker. Generosity does not have to be big to be felt.

textShort: Send an encouraging meme or GIF to a friend having a hard week.
textLong: If you know someone who has had a rough few days, send something lighthearted that says you are thinking of them. Pair it with a sincere line so it feels caring, not dismissive.

textShort: Send a voice note to someone you usually only text.
textLong: Pick someone you have only been texting. Record a 30–60 second voice note: say their name, one real thing you appreciate about them, and one honest question about how they are. Send it before you overthink it. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Congratulate someone online on something they worked for.
textLong: Find a post, story, or update about something someone earned or worked toward—a grade, job, project, recovery milestone, or creative release. Reply publicly with two or three specific sentences about what you admire. Skip generic praise like “so proud!!!” unless you add real detail. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Share one useful link with someone it actually fits.
textLong: Think of one person facing a concrete need—studying for a test, job hunting, learning a skill, or handling a task. Send them a single link (article, video, tool, or opportunity) and one sentence explaining why you thought of them. No mass forwards.

textShort: Leave a thoughtful comment on a friend's project or milestone.
textLong: Choose a friend's post about something they made, achieved, or shared. Write at least three sentences: what stood out, how it made you feel, and one encouraging line for what is next. Thoughtful comments take a minute and last much longer than a like.

textShort: Check in privately with someone who went quiet online.
textLong: Notice someone who used to talk in a group chat, server, or class thread but has gone quiet. Send a private message—no pressure to reply, just say you noticed and you care. Keep it short and genuine.

textShort: Send encouragement before something hard they face.
textLong: If you know someone has a test, interview, doctor visit, game, or tough conversation today, message them now. Wish them luck, remind them of one strength you see in them, and offer to hear how it went afterward.

textShort: Email or message a specific thank-you to a teacher or mentor.
textLong: Write a short thank-you to a teacher, coach, pastor, tutor, or mentor. Name one lesson or moment that stuck with you and how it helped you later. Send it even if years have passed—they rarely get notes like this.

textShort: Offer to proofread or give feedback on one page of writing.
textLong: Ask a friend or classmate if you can look at one page—an essay, email, application answer, or caption. Give two strengths and one clear suggestion. Set a time limit so you actually finish and send it back the same day.

textShort: Amplify a friend's project or fundraiser with a real caption.
textLong: Share a friend's shop, art, stream, channel, or fundraiser to your story or feed. Write one or two sentences about why you believe in them—not just “check this out.” Ask permission if it is personal or sensitive. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Send a warm message to someone you drifted from.
textLong: Think of someone you lost touch with—not to demand a full reunion, just to say you have been thinking of them and you hope they are doing okay. Keep it simple. No guilt trips, no long explanations unless they ask.

textShort: Mute one draining feed, then message someone you miss.
textLong: Unfollow, mute, or hide one account that leaves you more drained than inspired. Use the five minutes you would have scrolled to send one message to someone you have been meaning to reconnect with.

textShort: Tidy a shared space—and capture the before and after.
textLong: Pick one messy corner—a entryway table, shared bathroom counter, or club shelf—and spend ten minutes making it better for everyone. Take a quick before photo, then an after photo in Acts so you can see the difference you made.

textShort: Make or plate food for someone and photograph it.
textLong: Prepare something simple—a snack plate, toast, tea, or part of a meal—and set it out for someone you live with or work beside. Before they dig in, take a warm photo of what you made and save it as your act memory.

textShort: Photograph a small kindness you noticed today.
textLong: Look for a quiet good deed—a person helping someone, a thoughtful note, a cleaned-up spot. Take a photo that tells the story without embarrassing anyone (avoid close-ups of strangers’ faces unless they are fine with it).

textShort: Help a sibling with homework
textLong: Offer to help a sibling or family member with their homework. Even if it is just sitting nearby or encouraging them, showing that you are there can make a big difference. Snap a photo of your notes or workspace together (with their okay).

textShort: Help someone load groceries into their car
textLong: The next time you are in a parking lot or store, be on the lookout for someone who might need help loading their groceries into their car. Offer a quick, polite hand if the moment feels right. A quick photo of the loaded bags or your wave goodbye works as a memory.

textShort: Call or video chat with a grandparent or older relative.
textLong: Set aside fifteen minutes for a real conversation with a grandparent or older family member. Ask about their week, share a story from yours, or look at old photos together on video.

textShort: Bake or cook something and share it with neighbors or coworkers.
textLong: Make a simple batch of cookies, muffins, or a dish you enjoy and bring a portion to neighbors, classmates, or coworkers with a note that says you appreciate them.

textShort: Organize a small cleanup in a shared space you use.
textLong: Choose a locker area, club room, church hall, or park corner you use often. Spend twenty minutes picking up litter or straightening supplies. Leave it better than you found it.

textShort: Offer to tutor or study with someone who is struggling.
textLong: Reach out to a classmate or younger student who might be stuck on a subject you understand. Offer thirty minutes of help without making them feel embarrassed. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Write a recommendation or endorsement for someone.
textLong: Think of a peer, teammate, or coworker who deserves recognition. Write a short LinkedIn recommendation, a note to a coach or teacher about their character, or a genuine shout-out in a group chat.

textShort: Bring flowers or a small plant to brighten someone’s space.
textLong: Pick up a small bouquet, a potted plant, or even a single flower and give it to someone whose space could use cheer—a teacher’s desk, a parent’s kitchen, or a friend’s dorm room.

textShort: Plan a low-cost hangout focused on connection, not spending.
textLong: Invite one or two friends for a walk, board games at home, or a picnic instead of an expensive outing. The goal is quality time and making someone feel included.

textShort: Fix or mend something for someone at home.
textLong: Notice something broken—a loose hinge, a button missing, a bike chain—and offer to fix it for a family member or roommate. Practical help is a love language.

textShort: Schedule a video call with a friend you only text.
textLong: Pick a friend you have not seen on video in a long time. Send a calendar invite or concrete plan—“Tuesday 7pm for 20 minutes?”—and show up. Put phones on do-not-disturb except if kids or family need you. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Leave a short, honest review for a small business or creator.
textLong: Choose a local shop, app, book, album, or creator you genuinely like. Leave a brief review (two to four sentences): what you tried, what exceeded expectations, and who you would recommend it to. Honest and short beats long and vague. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Write sidewalk chalk encouragement and photograph it.
textLong: Use chalk to leave a short uplifting message on a sidewalk or driveway where it is allowed—something hopeful and kind. Photograph your message so you remember the words you shared with the neighborhood.

textShort: Lay out a care package, then deliver it.
textLong: Arrange a small care package on a table—snacks, a note, socks, tea—and photograph the flat lay. Then deliver it to someone having a hard week and save the photo as proof of your thoughtfulness.

textShort: Take a “study buddy” photo while you help someone learn.
textLong: Spend time helping someone with homework or a skill. Take a respectful photo of your notes, whiteboard, or workspace together (ask if they are comfortable being in frame).

textShort: Volunteer for a few hours with a local cause.
textLong: Find a local organization, school event, food pantry, or community cleanup that needs an extra pair of hands. Sign up or show up for a short shift and serve without expecting anything back. Even a few focused hours can make a real difference.

textShort: Write a letter to someone you appreciate.
textLong: Write a heartfelt letter to someone you appreciate. Tell them how they have impacted you or why you are thankful for them. Photograph the letter or envelope before you send it—it is a powerful way to encourage and connect.

textShort: Organize a donation drive with friends or your class.
textLong: Coordinate a small drive for food, coats, or school supplies. Set a simple goal, spread the word, and deliver items to a local charity or shelter together.

textShort: Visit someone who may be homebound or isolated.
textLong: Reach out to an elderly neighbor, relative, or community member who does not get many visitors. Bring tea, a card, or just your presence for a respectful visit.

textShort: Sponsor or support a cause you care about.
textLong: Choose a cause that matters to you—hunger, literacy, animals, disaster relief—and contribute what you can: a small donation, a fundraiser share, or an hour of volunteer time.

textShort: Create a care package for someone going through a hard season.
textLong: Assemble a small care package—snacks, a note, socks, tea, or things they need—and deliver it to a friend dealing with illness, grief, exams, or stress.

textShort: Teach someone a skill you are good at for free.
textLong: Offer a free lesson in something you know—an instrument, sport, language, art technique, or study strategy. One hour of generous teaching can open a door for someone else.

textShort: Document and celebrate acts of kindness you witnessed this month.
textLong: Write down three kind things you saw others do—or that you did—and share one story with a friend or post it privately in Acts. Celebrating goodness helps it spread. When you are done, snap a memory photo in Acts (your face or theirs only with permission).

textShort: Send someone a small album of old photos that would make them smile.
textLong: Dig through your camera roll or old chats for five photos or screenshots that would matter to one person—memories, inside jokes, or a season you shared. Send them in one message with a short caption for each. Nostalgia plus effort goes a long way.

textShort: Volunteer shift photo (with permission).
textLong: Serve at a food pantry, cleanup, or community event for at least an hour. Take one photo that captures the work—supplies sorted, bags handed off, or your team mid-task—with permission from the organizer and anyone visible.

textShort: Handwrite a card, photograph it, then mail or deliver it.
textLong: Write a thank-you or encouragement card by hand. Before you seal the envelope, photograph the card (cover any private addresses). Deliver or mail it to someone who needs to feel seen.
